Why this is in your inbox

Your publishing page sets out what you will and will not take. Here is where I honestly land on each one, including the one that goes against me.

Under $500k to finish fits

I am asking for $27,000. The game is playable start to finish today, so almost all of that is launch, marketing and the last polish pass rather than building the thing. It is a small number because there is not much left to build.

Under two years to release fits

The store page says Q1 2027, and that is a real date rather than a placeholder. I can extend it if the plan needs more runway. I started this in January 2024, so I am not looking for time to design a game, I am looking for time to land one that already exists.

Intense, stylized, with attitude fits

Sixteen robots, a shrinking platform, and a UFO that turns up mid round and helps itself to whoever is winning. Nothing here is gentle.

No generative AI assets in progress

Some menu and interface art in the current build was generated, and it is disclosed on my Steam page. All of it is coming out. Every generated asset gets replaced with handmade work and the store disclosure comes down with the last of them. Nothing else in the game was generated: not the bots, the arenas, the gameplay art, the audio or the code. I am telling you on slide one rather than letting you find it.

02

The game

RoboSquare: Recharged is an online multiplayer party game about hovering robots and the appalling things they do to each other. Up to 16 players drop into a lobby, play five randomly chosen minigames back to back, and score points every round until one bot is crowned champion.

Your bot floats, which sounds elegant until you realize floating things do not stop when you want them to. Momentum is your best weapon and your worst habit.

Mid round, things go wrong on purpose. Gravity gets lazy, bombs start falling, and a UFO turns up to help itself to whoever is winning. The empty seats fill themselves, so a full sixteen-bot brawl is always one click away.

There is no meta to study and no loadout to optimize. There is you, a floating metal square, and fifteen other people who would very much like you to be somewhere else. Ideally off the edge.

It ships as a finished game. Not Early Access, not a roadmap, not five modes arriving later.

A fifteenth is half built and not counted

04

Three buttons, eight ways it goes wrong

JUMPGet airborne, clear a gap, or leave the ground before someone else decides you should.
DASHClose distance fast, steal a checkpoint, or ram a stranger into a pit.
SLAMDrop out of the sky like a wrecking ball and launch everyone nearby into the sunset.

That is the whole control scheme. It takes about forty seconds to learn and considerably longer to stop being bad at, because every one of those three spends energy and every hit you take rattles you a little more.

Then, mid round and unannounced, the arena stops cooperating. These are the eight events currently in rotation:

Wind Storm Low Gravity Falling Bombs High Instability UFOs Cyber Pirates Clone Surge Nuke

Clone Surge gives everyone a duplicate wearing their own name and paint, which pops the moment anybody touches it. You cannot plan for any of it. That is the point.

05

Why it seats sixteen, and why the lobby never empties

Most party games seat four, or eight, or twelve. A group of six splits and two people watch. Sixteen seats means the whole Discord gets in at once. That was the design goal, not a number I happened to land on.

Sixteen robots colliding at once is a netcode problem before it is a design one. Recharged runs on Photon Quantum 3, a deterministic rollback simulation, which is the same class of technology fighting games use. Every client runs the same simulation and agrees on the result. It took longer than anything else in the project and it is the part I am proudest of.

The lobby is never empty. Any seat nobody is in gets filled, so a full sixteen-bot match is one click away at 3 am, or a year after launch, or the week everyone moves on to something else. It is designed to still be a good game with zero other people online, which is the thing that usually kills a small multiplayer launch about a month in.

I have shipped this game once already

I released RoboSquare on 31 December 2021. Free-to-play, and three modes that all came down to the same thing: push the other robot off the platform.

53,926lifetime unique players on Steam
77%positive across 249 reviews
29.92MSteam store page impressions

Two complaints came up over and over in those reviews. There is not enough of it, and I cannot get into a match. They were right on both counts and I could not fix either one without rebuilding the whole thing. That is what Recharged is.

07

The Fall Guys slot is open

Almost every party game that broke out recently is co-op against the environment. PEAK is the reason a lot of people take the category seriously at all, so I am not going to try to sell you on the genre.

What almost nobody is shipping is competitive party PvP. That is the Fall Guys slot, and it has been sitting open for years while everything adjacent to it sold enormously. The category is not crowded. It is crowded next door.

The obvious objection is that this is a Fall Guys clone. My answer is that Fall Guys is one obstacle-course format at 60 players with no rollback, and this is five distinct competitive modes at sixteen with a lobby that cannot go empty. I chose the comparison, and it is doing work for me.

Fall GuysThe anchor everyone understands in one sentence, and the slot nobody has refilled.
Human: Fall FlatPhysics comedy multiplayer sells for a decade, not a launch week.
Meccha ChameleonTwo million copies in five days in 2026. The audience is right there and it is buying.
Super Battle Golf100k in two days. Proof the PvP half of this category still converts.
08

How it makes money, and why it is built that way

Premium purchase up front at $5.99 USD. On top of that, cosmetics only, and nothing that changes a match.

Crates and keys both drop from playing, daily, for everyone. If you do not want to wait, you can buy keys. That is the whole monetization, and the earnable keys part is the bit that matters, because it is what separates this from the games people are angry about.

There is a reason it is built that way rather than outsourced. The first RoboSquare's monetization was handled through an outside partner. They dissolved without paying out, and that was the end of the first game's economy.

I built this one myself, and everything in it can be earned by playing. I would rather own it and keep it small than hand it to someone else again.

The ask

What I want

  • $27,000 to finish, launch and market it
  • The Q1 2027 window already on the store page, extended only if the plan needs it
  • Marketing reach and playtest volume, which is what I cannot buy with evenings

What I am not asking for

  • Design help. The game works, and I would rather be told it is wrong than have it redesigned
  • An Early Access runway. It ships finished
  • Years. It is close

Where I am flexible

  • Revenue share and recoupment structure, entirely open
  • Milestones, as long as the acceptance criteria are objective
  • Console porting, if you want it. I have not started it
  • IP stays with Fizzostia. That is the one I would rather not move on

A playable build is ready now and I will send it the moment you want it, along with Steam keys and raw capture. There is no vertical slice to schedule, because the whole game is the slice.

11

What is wrong with this pitch

You will find all of these anyway, so here they are with my answers attached.

  • Generated UI art is in the current build and disclosed on the store page. All of it is being replaced with handmade work and the disclosure comes down with it. Until that is finished, the honest version is that the work is underway, not done.
  • There is no wishlist curve yet. The store page went live on 4 September 2026 and the count is about 25. Nothing in this deck is validated by pre-release traction, because there has not been time for any.
  • One person. There is no second engineer, so the bus factor is one. Whatever the plan is, it has to survive that.
  • Online only. No local play and no Remote Play Together, so the couch audience is not addressable without work that is not currently scoped.
  • Live multiplayer costs money forever. Filled seats keep the game playable at any population, which solves the design half of that problem. It does not solve the hosting bill.
